name: Volunteer Management
objectives: For one volunteer role your organization needs, write a role description that says the impact, the tasks, the time, the skills and who the volunteer reports to, with all five parts and an opening sentence about impact

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing a volunteer role description
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear, inviting role description for one volunteer job.
This lesson builds toward: For one volunteer role your organization needs, you will write a role description that says the impact, the tasks, the time, the skills and who the volunteer reports to, with all five parts and an opening sentence about impact.
Volunteers do their best when they know exactly what is asked of them. A role description is like a short job description: it says what the role is, why it matters, what the volunteer will do, the time needed, the skills or traits needed, any training or screening, and who they report to.
Make it inviting. Start with the impact: "Help 200 families get groceries every Saturday." Be honest about the time, including how long you hope they stay (one event, or six months). Offer short, flexible roles as well as long ones; many people can give two hours but not every week.
Write a separate description for each role. A food bank might have greeters, sorters, drivers and a data-entry helper, each with different needs.
Step by step:
- Name the role and say why it matters.
- List what the volunteer will do.
- Say when, how long, and for how many months.
- List skills, traits and any age limits.
- Note training, screening and who they report to.
Words to know:
- Role description: a short write-up of a volunteer job: what, when, why, and what's needed.
- Volunteer coordinator: the person who recruits, organizes and supports volunteers.
Try it now: Pick one volunteer role your organization needs. Write its role description using all five parts. Start with one sentence about the impact.
You can now write a clear role description that tells volunteers exactly what is asked and why it matters.

check.q: What is a volunteer role description?
options: A short job description that says what the role is, why it matters and what is asked
check.why: A role description tells volunteers exactly what is asked of them, like a short job description.

check.q: Your description says "Help out sometimes." What do you add first?
options: A list of every rule you have
When and for how long, and the impact the role makes
check.why: Volunteers need honest time details and a reason the role matters.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Recruiting and screening volunteers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Recruit volunteers for a role and choose the right screening steps for it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a volunteer role and who it serves, you will write a recruiting message and choose the screening steps that match the role's risk, including references and a background check with written permission for any role with children or vulnerable adults.
The most common reason people volunteer is that someone asked them. Ask personally, through current volunteers, places of worship, schools, employers with volunteer programs, community boards and social media. Share the role description and a simple way to sign up.
Screening protects the people you serve, your volunteers and your organization. Match it to the risk of the role. Every role: an application with contact details and an emergency contact, and a short conversation. Higher-risk roles, especially any work with children or vulnerable adults (older adults, people with disabilities), also need reference checks and a background check, done with the person's written permission through a reputable provider.
Rules about background checks for volunteers differ by state and by program, and your insurer may have requirements. Ask your insurance company and a lawyer what applies to you. Add safety rules too: for example, no adult is alone and out of sight with a child, and every concern is reported to a named person.
Step by step:
- Ask people personally; use current volunteers and community partners.
- Share the role description and an easy sign-up.
- For every role: application, emergency contact and a short talk.
- For roles with children or vulnerable adults: references and a background check with written permission.
- Check state rules and your insurer's requirements.
- Set safety rules, like no adult alone and out of sight with a child.
Words to know:
- Screening: the steps you take to check a volunteer is right and safe for a role.
- Background check: a search of public records, such as criminal records, done with a person's permission.
- Vulnerable adult: an adult who may need extra protection, such as some older adults or people with disabilities.
Try it now: For the role you described in Lesson 1, write a short recruiting message and list three places you will share it. Then list the screening steps the role needs and explain why, based on its risk.
You can now recruit volunteers personally and choose screening steps that match the risk of each role.

check.q: What should every volunteer role, even a low-risk one, include in screening?
options: An application with contact details and an emergency contact, and a short talk
check.why: Every role gets an application, an emergency contact and a short conversation; higher-risk roles add more.

check.q: A new role has volunteers reading with older adults in a care home. What do you add?
options: References and a background check with written permission
A social media post about the residents
check.why: Roles with vulnerable adults need reference checks and a background check done with permission.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Onboarding and training volunteers
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a short orientation and role training that gets new volunteers ready and welcome.
This lesson builds toward: For new volunteers in your role, you will plan a 30-minute orientation and train the role in four steps: explain, show, try and feedback, covering safety, privacy, sign-in and how to cancel.
The first day decides whether many volunteers come back. Onboarding is everything that happens from "yes" to being confident in the role: a welcome message, an orientation, training for the role and a friendly first shift.
An orientation covers the mission and who you serve, where things are, who to ask, safety and emergency steps, privacy rules (for example, not sharing clients' names or photos), and how to sign in and cancel a shift. Role training shows them how to do the job: explain, show, let them try, then give feedback. A short checklist or video helps them remember.
Pair new volunteers with an experienced buddy for their first shift, and check in afterward: "How did it go? What was confusing?"
Step by step:
- Send a welcome message with time, place and who to ask for.
- Hold an orientation: mission, layout, safety, privacy, sign-in and cancelling.
- Train the role: explain, show, let them try, give feedback.
- Give a simple checklist.
- Pair them with a buddy.
- Check in after the first shift.
Words to know:
- Onboarding: the steps that help a new volunteer get started and feel welcome.
- Orientation: a first session that explains the organization, rules and safety.
- Confidentiality: keeping private information about the people you serve private.
Try it now: Write a 30-minute orientation outline for your role, with times for each part. Then write the role's training as four steps: explain, show, try, feedback.
You can now onboard and train new volunteers so they are safe, confident and want to return.

options: Only the first email you send
Everything from "yes" to feeling confident in the role
check.why: Onboarding includes the welcome, orientation, role training and a friendly first shift.

check.q: A new volunteer starts Saturday. What helps most on the first shift?
options: Pair them with an experienced buddy and check in afterward
Leave them alone to figure it out
Skip the orientation to save time
check.why: A buddy gives them someone to ask, and a check-in shows what was confusing.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Scheduling and supervising volunteers
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a volunteer schedule with backups and supervise volunteers in a supportive way.
This lesson builds toward: Using a spreadsheet, shared calendar or paper, you will build a one-month schedule with a named shift lead, backups and a reminder message, with every shift covered and a lead named for each.
Make the schedule easy to see and easy to change. A shared calendar, a free sign-up tool or a simple spreadsheet works. Post shifts early, send a reminder a day or two before, and make cancelling simple so people tell you instead of just not showing up. Plan a backup list for key shifts.
Every shift should have a named supervisor or lead volunteer who welcomes people, gives out tasks, answers questions and handles problems. Supervising volunteers is like managing staff, but lighter: clear tasks, regular check-ins, and quick, kind feedback.
If a volunteer is not working out, talk privately, be specific and ask what would help. Sometimes a different role fits better. If someone breaks safety or conduct rules, follow your policy, which may include ending their volunteer role.
Step by step:
- Use a shared calendar, sign-up tool or spreadsheet.
- Post shifts early and send reminders.
- Make cancelling easy; keep a backup list.
- Name a supervisor for every shift.
- Give clear tasks and quick, kind feedback.
- Handle problems privately; follow policy for safety breaches.
Words to know:
- Shift: a set block of time when a volunteer works.
- Shift lead: the person in charge of volunteers during a shift.
- Backup list: volunteers you can call when someone cancels.
Try it now: Make a one-month schedule for your role in a spreadsheet or on paper: dates, shift times, volunteer names, a named shift lead and two backup names. Write the reminder message you will send.
You can now build a volunteer schedule with reminders and backups, and supervise volunteers in a clear, supportive way.

options: A list of volunteers who quit
People you can call when someone cancels a key shift
check.why: A backup list keeps key shifts covered when plans change.

check.q: A volunteer keeps making mistakes in their role. What do you do first?
options: Tell the whole team about it
Talk privately, be specific and ask what would help
Stop scheduling them without saying why
check.why: Handle problems privately and kindly; a different role may fit better.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Recognition and retention
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan recognition that fits your volunteers and spot why volunteers leave.
This lesson builds toward: For the volunteers you manage, you will plan specific recognition and identify the common reasons volunteers leave, with one small thank-you and one bigger moment.
Volunteers often stop coming because they felt unneeded, poorly organized, untrained, or unthanked, or because life got busy. Keeping them is cheaper and easier than finding new ones.
Thank people often and specifically: "Your Saturday shifts helped us pack 600 boxes this month." Share stories of the impact, with permission from the people served. Mix small, everyday thanks (a note, a shout-out, a text) with bigger moments (an appreciation event, a certificate, a reference letter for a job or school).
Ask volunteers what they want: new skills, friends, leadership, flexibility. Offer growth, like training new volunteers or leading a shift. Ask people who leave why, and use what you learn.
Step by step:
- Thank people often and specifically.
- Share impact stories, with permission.
- Mix small thanks with bigger moments.
- Ask what each volunteer wants from the experience.
- Offer growth roles.
- Ask people who leave why.
Words to know:
- Retention: keeping volunteers coming back over time.
- Recognition: showing volunteers that their work is noticed and valued.
Try it now: Write two recognition ideas for your volunteers: one small thank-you you can give this week and one bigger moment for this year. Then write three questions you will ask a volunteer about what they want from the role.
You can now recognize volunteers in ways that matter to them and act on the reasons volunteers leave.

check.q: Which is a common reason volunteers stop coming?
check.why: Feeling unneeded, poorly organized, untrained or unthanked often makes volunteers leave.

check.q: A loyal volunteer says they want to build leadership skills. What do you offer?
options: A chance to lead a shift or train new volunteers
check.why: Growth roles such as leading a shift help keep volunteers who want more.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Tracking volunteer hours
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a simple system to track volunteer hours and use the numbers.
This lesson builds toward: For one volunteer role, you will set up a sign-in sheet or spreadsheet that tracks volunteer hours and use the totals, recording name, date, start, end, hours and role while keeping records private.
Track who volunteered, when, for how long and in what role. A paper sign-in sheet copied into a spreadsheet works for small groups; a free form or volunteer app can work for larger ones. Keep it simple so people actually sign in and out.
The numbers help you: they show impact in grant reports and to your board, help you plan staffing, and help you thank your most faithful volunteers. Many volunteers also need proof of hours for school, scholarships, court or community-service requirements, or job applications. Be ready to sign a letter or form confirming their hours.
Keep volunteer records private and safe, and only collect what you need. A tax note for volunteers: the IRS says the value of volunteer time is not tax-deductible, though some unreimbursed out-of-pocket costs may be. Point volunteers to IRS Publication 526 and a tax professional rather than giving tax advice.
Step by step:
- Choose a sign-in method: paper sheet, form or app.
- Record name, date, start and end time, and role.
- Enter the data in one spreadsheet each week.
- Add up hours by volunteer, by month and by program.
- Use the totals in reports, planning and thank-yous.
- Keep records private; sign proof-of-hours letters when asked.
Words to know:
- Sign-in sheet: a simple form where volunteers write their name and the time they start and finish.
- Proof of hours: a signed letter or form confirming how many hours someone volunteered.
- Grant report: a report to a funder showing what was done with their money.
Official sources:
- IRS Publication 526, Charitable Contributions
Try it now: Final task: build your volunteer kit for one role: the role description, recruiting message and screening steps, a 30-minute orientation outline, a monthly schedule with a shift lead, two recognition ideas, and a sign-in sheet or spreadsheet with columns for name, date, start, end, hours and role.
You can now track volunteer hours simply and use the numbers for reports, planning, thank-yous and proof of hours.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Role description Missing the time, tasks or who they report to. All five parts, opening with the impact. Also offers a short, flexible option for people with less time. Recruiting and screening No screening, or a role with children or vulnerable adults has no background check. A recruiting message and screening matched to the role's risk, with written permission for checks. Also adds safety rules and notes to check with the insurer and a lawyer. Orientation and training No orientation plan, or safety and privacy are missing. A 30-minute outline with times, covering safety, privacy, sign-in and cancelling, plus explain, show, try, feedback. Also includes a buddy and a check-in after the first shift. Schedule and supervision Shifts lack a lead or there are no backups. A one-month schedule with a named shift lead, two backups and a reminder message. Also says how volunteers cancel and who handles problems. Recognition and hours No thank-you plan or no way to track hours. One small and one bigger recognition idea, and a sign-in sheet with name, date, start, end, hours and role. Also says how the hour totals will be used in reports and thank-yous. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: To show impact in grant and board reports and to plan staffing
Because volunteers are paid by the hour
check.why: Hour totals show impact, help planning and help you thank faithful volunteers.

check.q: A volunteer asks if they can deduct the value of their time on their taxes. What do you do?
options: Say yes, at any hourly rate
Point them to IRS Publication 526 and a tax professional
check.why: The lesson says not to give tax advice; point volunteers to IRS Publication 526 and a tax professional.
